title: Training: Defeating Narratives of Division
content:
This training covers local organising initiatives and tools including mapping community divisions, bridging them through stories of “us,” and learning from the example of Cable Street. Participants explore theories of change, transformative conversations and strategic choices for change-makers while learning how to build democratic traditions, and win against provocation while countering divisive narratives.

This resource was developed by Ella Baker School of Organizing.

“Exploiting genuine resentments about the cost of living, the housing crisis and insecure employment prospects (and dishonestly blaming migrants and minorities for all ills), these narratives of division are growing. However, they can and must be stopped. By organising together in our communities we can start to address the root causes of people’s frustration and resentment, that the far-right are parasitic on.”

title: Fighting the Far Right
content:
This article summarizes an event hosted by the Global Grassroots Support Network (GGSN) on Fighting the Far Right, case studies + discussion, held on the 24th of September, 2026.

35 people joined us from Canada, Mexico, the UK, Belgium, France, Kenya, Uganda and India. The session was moderated by Kenzie Harris (GGSN coordinator) and the event featured the following speakers:

  • Natasha Adams (Thinking Doing Change, natasha.adamscampaigns@gmail.com) – UK
  • Kate Turner (Building Power Network, bpn-rpc@protonmail.com) – Canada
  • Jacob Okumu (GGSN, jacob@blueprintsfc.org) – Kenya
  • Anonymous speaker – India

    • Speakers gave an overview of the context in their countries, and shared specific examples to further understand the context and how grassroots/NGOs are responding. The discussion reviewed the Gen Z protests in India, moving towards what we want (not just resisting what we don’t want) and included tips for holding coalition building/strategic gatherings to fight the right collectively. The descriptions provided below mostly reflect the wording the speakers themselves used.
